candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — minor consent/confidentiality for STI services
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize minors' nationwide authority to consent for STI services while applying jurisdiction-specific confidentiality, notification, age, and service provisions at the point of care.

options.A: Federal law requires parental consent for all STI testing and treatment of minors, so care cannot begin until a parent authorizes it.
options.B: All 50 states and the District of Columbia allow minors to consent for their own STI services; confidentiality, notification, and some age- or service-specific provisions still vary, so current jurisdiction law and policy must be applied.
options.C: Minors can consent to STI testing nationwide but never to treatment, so a parent must authorize medication in every jurisdiction.
options.D: Only emancipated minors may independently consent to STI services; non-emancipated adolescents always require a parent to be present.

candidate.rationale: CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines state that all 50 states and the District of Columbia explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services and that no state requires parental consent for STI care. CDC also notes variation in age provisions for specified services and important confidentiality and parental-notification issues. B accurately combines the nationwide STI-consent principle with the need to apply current jurisdiction-specific details. A, C, and D impose universal restrictions that CDC says are incorrect.
candidate.source_claim_supported: All 50 states and DC explicitly allow minors to consent for their own STI services; no state requires parental consent for STI care; age provisions for specified services and confidentiality/notification considerations vary.
candidate.source_document_title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021 — Adolescents
candidate.source_locator: Adolescents — Legal Issues and Confidentiality; CDC STI Treatment Guidelines landing page identifying the 2021 guideline as current clinical guidance.
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidate.source_version_date: 2021 guideline remains CDC's current STI Treatment Guidelines in 2026
candidate.stem: A 16-year-old seeks testing and treatment for a suspected sexually transmitted infection and asks whether parental consent is required. Which response is most accurate?
